outcome.answer:
It is difficult for neural networks to learn highly ambiguous token distributions because higher ambiguity makes the target next-token distribution harder to represent and fit accurately. In particular, more ambiguous next-token distributions require more capacity to store, larger embeddings to represent, more optimization steps, and they amplify token-sampling noise, all of which makes accurate learning challenging [1].

Relatedly, when learning involves conditional uncertainty, models may first lock onto easier marginal structure rather than the full conditional distribution; in a controlled setting with K-fold ambiguity, the model learns the marginal first and only later collapses to the full conditional via a sharp transition. This suggests that ambiguous conditional structure can stabilize simpler, lower-accuracy solutions before the network can represent the full conditional behavior [2].

These effects differ in focus: [1] attributes difficulty directly to ambiguity increasing representational/learning burden and sampling noise, while [2] studies a conditional-learning dynamic where ambiguity produces an initial plateau for the marginal before conditional learning completes.
